title: US proposes up to 25% tariff on Indian goods, 17% with a deal; India rejects 'excess capacity' finding
dek: Washington named India among 14 economies it accuses of manufacturing overcapacity, putting it above Bangladesh and below only Vietnam. The rates are proposals, with hearings in January.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The United States has proposed tariffs of up to 25% on all goods from India, the second-highest rate among the 14 economies it accused on Wednesday of building up "structural excess capacity" in manufacturing. The rate would fall to 17% if India signs a trade agreement that answers Washington's complaints. India's commerce ministry rejected the finding and said trade concerns should be settled through bilateral talks.

The proposal, from the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR), is not yet in force. It opens a comment period to 5 January 2027, with public hearings from 25 January. But it sets the terms of the next round of India-US trade talks: a gap of eight percentage points between the default rate and the rate on offer for a deal, and a list of complaints about India's industrial policy that runs from steel and solar panels to medicines.

## What happened

USTR Jamieson Greer announced determinations in 14 of the 16 investigations opened on 11 March under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which lets Washington impose duties on countries whose practices it judges "unreasonable or discriminatory" and burdensome to US commerce. The 14 are China, the European Union, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, Singapore, Cambodia, Bangladesh and Switzerland. USTR made no determination for Mexico or Norway.

"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing," Mr Greer said in the USTR's release, adding that the action aimed to "level the playing field for American workers."

In its Federal Register notice on India, USTR said India's "acts, policies, and practices" were unreasonable and burdened US commerce. It cited national industrial plans to expand manufacturing, what it called inadequate labour protections, financial repression, market-access barriers, and a failure to address imports and investment from "non-market economies", chiefly China. It named four sectors: steel, solar, health (pharmaceuticals and medical devices) and information and communications technology.

The notice gives some of the numbers behind the finding. It says India's solar module capacity has reached roughly 140-160 gigawatts, about three times annual domestic demand of 40-50 GW. It cites a forecast that China and India together will account for 80% of Asia's additional steelmaking capacity in the coming years. It says India's imports of intermediate inputs from China rose by $44 billion, or 97%, between 2017 and 2025, and argues that cheap Chinese inputs make Indian downstream products "artificially" competitive. It also notes that India supplies up to 61% of generic solid oral drug doses sold in the US, according to "certain reports", while depending on China for many active pharmaceutical ingredients.

The proposed action is tariffs "of up to 25 percent on all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs." USTR said it would consider adjusting the rate to account for other duties India already faces, or setting it at 17% "were India to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations."

Several categories would be exempt, including goods already covered by separate national-security (Section 232) tariffs: steel, aluminium and copper articles, cars and car parts, trucks, wood products, patented medicines and semiconductors.

## How India compares

Only Vietnam faces a higher default rate, of up to 35% (20% with a deal). China's default rate is up to 20%, with some goods at 10% and others exempt, and up to 40% if its commitments are judged unsatisfactory. Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand face up to 18%, and the EU, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan 15%.

That ranking matters as much as the rate itself. India has said it wants a lower tariff than competing exporters, according to reports, and the proposal puts its default rate seven points above Bangladesh's. For eastern India's garment and leather exporters, who compete with Bangladesh for the same US orders, a 25% rate against 18% would be a clear disadvantage. Even the 17% deal rate would only just undercut Bangladesh's default.

## Background

Washington rebuilt its tariff regime this year after the US Supreme Court struck down, in February, the tariffs President Donald Trump had imposed under emergency-powers law, according to reports. The administration turned to Section 301, which has no ceiling on rates. A separate Section 301 investigation into forced labour in supply chains led to duties of 10% or 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners from 24 July; India was given the 10% rate. The new duties would be charged net of those.

India and the US announced an interim trade framework in February, but the court ruling sent it back to negotiators. Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said on 18 November that the deal was "more or less finalised" but would not be signed until the US settled its new tariff structure, according to reports. India argued throughout the investigation that it has no structural excess capacity: USTR's own notice records India's submission that its Production Linked Incentive schemes aim at self-reliance and should not be seen as "creating manufacturing capacity untethered from demand", and that its steel and solar capacity serves a growing domestic market.

## What they are saying

The Ministry of Commerce and Industry said on Wednesday that it had taken note of the determination and was examining it, according to reports. It said India had told USTR during the proceedings that it "did not have structural excess capacity in any sector", that trade concerns should be handled through bilateral negotiations, and that the government remained committed to working with Washington towards "an early conclusion" of the bilateral trade agreement.

USTR said it invites comments on the proposed action and on "any possible adjustment to the rate to be applied following a final agreement."

## What happens next

The rates can still change. Written comments and requests to testify are due by 5 January 2027 on USTR's docket USTR-2026-0731, and the Section 301 Committee will open hearings at the US International Trade Commission in Washington on 25 January. No effective date has been set. Reports said the duties are likely to face legal challenges in US courts.

For New Delhi the decision is now clear-cut: sign a deal that USTR considers "responsive" to its findings and take the 17% rate, or contest a 25% one. Whether the agreement Mr Agrawal described as nearly finished meets that test is the question for the coming weeks.

## Key numbers

- Up to 25%: proposed default tariff on Indian goods
- 17%: rate if India signs a responsive trade agreement
- 18%: Bangladesh's proposed default rate
- 140-160 GW: India's solar module capacity, according to USTR
- $44 billion: rise in India's intermediate imports from China, 2017-2025, according to USTR
- 5 January 2027: deadline for comments
- 25 January 2027: public hearings begin
